Planner conversation toolkit · Canada and British Columbia

Explain investing clearly, and honestly.

Seven short visual conversations. Pick the client’s question, adjust the chart together, and let the talking points guide you.

  • Historical data published, dated and sourced
  • Illustration assumptions, not a forecast or history

For conversations, not promises. Investment returns and recoveries are not guaranteed, risk matters, and mutual funds are not suitable for everyone.

Conversations

  1. 01Why invest at all?Inflation and cash
  2. 02Why a monthly plan?Regular contributions

Sources and method

01Inflation and cash

“Why not just keep it in savings?”

Cash is the right home for an emergency fund and money needed soon. Over longer periods, rising prices quietly shrink what savings can buy.

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“A savings account keeps your dollars safe, but inflation can shrink what they buy. Investing aims for growth that can help offset inflation over time, with the risk that values fall, especially over short periods.”
Keep it balanced
Cash and GICs have a real job: stability and money you will need soon. Investing makes sense for money that can stay put through ups and downs.
Ask
“Which part of this money might you need in the next two or three years?”
NextWhy a monthly plan?

02Regular contributions

“Why set up a monthly plan instead of waiting?”

A pre-authorized contribution plan (PAC) turns investing into a habit. Buying the same dollar amount each month also means more units are bought when prices are lower.

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“You don’t have to guess the right day. The plan buys a little every month, including the months that feel uncomfortable.”
Keep it honest
A monthly plan is mostly about habit and cash flow. With a lump sum already in hand, investing it now gives every dollar more time invested, while spreading it out can feel easier but leaves cash waiting. Neither approach is guaranteed to come out ahead.
Practical
Line the PAC up with payday, and revisit the amount when income changes.
PreviousWhy invest at all?NextWhat if markets fall?

03Volatility and recovery

“What happens when the market drops?”

Falls are a normal part of investing, and the range of outcomes is widest over short periods. A plan a client can stick with through a decline matters more than one that looks best on paper.

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“A 30% drop needs about a 43% gain to get back. That is why we match the mix to how much of a fall you can live with, not just the return you want.”
Keep it honest
Recoveries have happened after past declines, but they are not guaranteed, and they can be slow. Someone who needs the money during a decline can lock in a loss.
Ask
“If this account fell by a fifth next year, what would you want to do?”
PreviousWhy a monthly plan?NextWhat does the ride feel like?

04A hypothetical balanced fund

“What does the ride actually feel like?”

An average return sounds smooth; year-by-year results are not. This hypothetical example uses invented returns, already net of expenses, to show the difference between the average and the path.

Before looking at a real fund

Read the real Fund Facts together

For any fund you discuss, its Fund Facts document shows the risk rating, year-by-year returns for up to ten years, the best and worst 3-month returns and its costs [4]. Use the fund company’s own, current figures rather than recalculating them.

Distributions are taxable outside registered plans

Funds usually pay out income and realized gains, often once a year. In a non-registered account those distributions are taxable in the year they are paid even when they are reinvested, and even in a year when the fund’s value fell. Inside a TFSA or RRSP they are not taxed when paid.

Compare like with like

Compare total returns over identical periods, after costs, in the same currency, and only between investments with similar objectives.

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“Even a balanced fund has down years. The average only shows up for people who stay in through the bumps, so let’s choose a mix you can stay with.”
Keep it honest
These numbers are invented. For a real fund, use its current Fund Facts and the fund company’s published returns, and remember past returns do not predict future returns.
Ask
“Looking at the worst year here, how would you have felt, and what would you have done?”
PreviousWhat if markets fall?NextWhy not just pick winners?

05Diversification

“Why not just buy the best few stocks?”

Owning many investments that don’t move in lockstep reduces the damage any one can do. It can’t remove the risk that the whole market falls, which is why the stock and bond mix matters too.

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“Diversification means no single company can sink the plan. It won’t stop a market-wide fall, so we also choose how much goes in stocks versus bonds.”
Watch for
Concentration that clients may not count: employer shares, a single sector, or one country. Look at the whole household picture.
PreviousWhat does the ride feel like?NextWhere does a balanced fund sit?

06Asset classes compared

“Isn’t a balanced fund always safely in the middle?”

A balanced portfolio blends bonds and stocks, so its range of outcomes is narrower than stocks alone. It can still lose money, and in a given year it can trail cash or sit near the bottom of the table.

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“A balanced fund smooths the ride but doesn’t remove it. In a year when stocks and bonds fall together, it falls too, and cash can come out ahead.”
Keep it honest
These are teaching assumptions. For a real fund or index, use its own published results and compare like with like: same period, same currency, total return, after costs.
Ask
“Which of these years would worry you most, and what would you want to do in it?”
PreviousWhy not just pick winners?NextWhy not just buy a GIC?

07After-tax comparison · BC 2026

“Why not just buy a GIC?”

A GIC (guaranteed investment certificate) offers a known rate. Eligible GIC deposits at an insured institution are protected, principal and interest, within deposit-insurance limits. A balanced fund offers growth potential with no guarantee. Outside registered accounts they are also taxed differently, which this tool shows.

How each kind of return is taxed
ReturnNon-registeredTFSARRSP or RRIF
GIC interestTaxed every year at the full rate, even when a compounding GIC has not paid it out [9]Not taxed [23]Not taxed until withdrawn; withdrawals taxed as income [24]
Fund interest and foreign incomeTaxed in the year paid at the full rate, even if reinvested [9]Not taxedSame as all RRSP money
Fund Canadian dividendsGrossed up, then reduced by the dividend tax credit, so usually taxed less than interest [11][12][13]Not taxedNo dividend credit: withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income
Fund capital gains distributionsHalf is taxable, in the year paid [14]Not taxedSame as all RRSP money
Growth in unit valueNot taxed until units are sold; then half of the gain above the adjusted cost base is taxable [10]Not taxedSame as all RRSP money

Talking points Hidden in client view

Try saying
“A GIC tells you exactly what you’ll get. A balanced fund might earn more, but it can also lose, and nobody can promise which.”
Keep it honest
Any advantage for the fund here comes entirely from the return you assume. Try a low or negative return too, and point to the break-even rate.
Ask
“If this money dropped 10% in the first year, would that change your plans?”

  14. Prime Minister of Canada, 21 March 2025: the proposed increase to the capital gains inclusion rate is cancelled (the inclusion rate remains one-half). Source (opens in a new tab)
  15. Canada Revenue Agency, Tax rates and income brackets for individuals: current year (2026 federal and BC tables). Source (opens in a new tab)
  16. Government of British Columbia, B.C. basic personal income tax rates (2026 brackets; updated 17 April 2026). Source (opens in a new tab)
  17. Government of British Columbia, Budget tax changes (updated 26 February 2026): lowest personal income tax rate rises from 5.06% to 5.60% for 2026 and later years. Source (opens in a new tab)
  18. Legislative Assembly of British Columbia, Bill 2 – 2026, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026 (third reading text): section 37 replaces “5.06%” with “5.6%”, in force January 1, 2026. Source (opens in a new tab)

How the illustrations work
  • Returns are effective annual rates, compounded monthly for monthly plans and yearly elsewhere; contributions are made at each month-end.
  • The outcome range uses independent, normally distributed annual log returns. Real markets have fatter tails: big moves happen more often than this model expects.
  • Diversification uses portfolio volatility = σ × √(1/n + (1 − 1/n) × ρ) for equal holdings; the asset-class comparison uses σ = √(wᵀΣw) with assumed correlations.
  • The GIC comparison applies BC 2026 statutory marginal rates to each kind of income in the year it is taxed: interest and foreign income at the full rate, eligible dividends after the gross-up and both dividend tax credits, capital gains at a one-half inclusion rate. The GIC compounds yearly at its first-term rate, then renews at the assumed renewal rate at each maturity. The fund’s lower and higher results use the 8-in-10 range of its average yearly return (middle case ± 1.28 × the balanced portfolio’s assumed volatility ÷ √years). RRSP/RRIF results compare balances before withdrawal tax, because the contribution was deducted.

General education to support a conversation, not personal financial, tax or investment advice, and not an offer of any product. It does not discuss or show the performance of any specific fund. Suitability depends on each client’s goals, time horizon, risk tolerance and full financial picture.
